cases.brief: An undergraduate note whose central purpose is to explain the telescoping mechanism behind the sum of the first n odd numbers.
cases.draft: Introduction. We study 1 + 3 + ... + (2n-1). Setup. An integer is called positive when it is greater than zero. For example, 1 is positive. So are 2 and 3. Throughout, n is positive. The symbol n labels the last index, and the indices begin at 1. Thus the first index is 1 and the last index is n. Theorem. The sum is n^2. Proof. This follows by algebra. Conclusion. Telescoping is the useful mechanism.

cases.brief: An undergraduate note whose central purpose is to explain the telescoping mechanism behind the sum of the first n odd numbers.
cases.draft: Why do successive odd numbers add up to a square? The useful observation is that the kth odd number is the difference between consecutive squares: 2k-1 = k^2-(k-1)^2. For a positive integer n, summing these differences from k=1 to n cancels each intermediate square, leaving n^2-0^2. Hence 1+3+...+(2n-1)=n^2. For instance, 1+3+5=9. The same cancellation method applies whenever summands can be written as consecutive differences.

cases.brief: A beginner-facing explanation of why division by a positive quantity preserves an inequality; sign reasoning is the main teaching objective.
cases.draft: Suppose a <= b and c > 0. Since b-a >= 0 and 1/c > 0, their product (b-a)/c is nonnegative. Therefore b/c-a/c >= 0, which is precisely a/c <= b/c. Positivity of c matters: division by a negative number would reverse the inequality. For example, dividing 1 <= 2 by -1 gives -1 >= -2.
